messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 62

He is 67, a hotel manager who has spent most of his adult life solving other people’s problems with a calm voice and a practiced smile. Before the robbery, he describes himself as steady, social, and proud of being the person staff could count on when a guest became upset or something went wrong late at night. He has been married for decades, and he and his wife have a settled routine that once felt comforting in its predictability. He used to leave the hotel after evening shift without much thought, often carrying the day’s receipts or paperwork to his car, mentally reviewing staffing issues for the next morning.

The robbery happens on an ordinary night, which is part of what makes it stay with him. He locks up his office later than usual and walks through the side lot behind the hotel, thinking about a no-show employee and a plumbing issue on the third floor. He notices someone moving toward him but assumes at first it is a guest asking for directions or a ride-share driver looking for the front entrance. The man closes the distance quickly. He is suddenly shoved hard against a wall. A hand grabs his jacket, and then he sees the weapon. Even now, when he tells the story, he does not linger on details of the mugger’s face; what he remembers with perfect clarity is the cold certainty that he is about to die in a parking lot behind his own workplace. He hands over his wallet, his phone, the envelope he is carrying. The man demands more, curses at him, pats him down roughly, and runs. He stands there for several seconds after, unable to move, his legs weak and his heart pounding so hard it makes him nauseated.

In the hours after, he does what he has always done in a crisis: he shifts into managerial mode. He calls police, answers questions, reviews security footage, contacts ownership, reassures shaken staff. It is not until he gets home and sees his wife waiting up for him that his control slips. He cannot stop trembling. When she reaches for him, he flinches before he can help it. That reaction embarrasses him more than he can explain.

At first, he tells himself he is lucky and should be over it soon. Instead, the nights become difficult. He lies awake replaying the moment he saw the weapon, hearing the man’s voice as if it is in the room. When he does sleep, he wakes abruptly, drenched in sweat, disoriented and alert to every sound outside the house. He begins checking the locks repeatedly before bed. If a car door slams in the street, his whole body tightens. His wife notices that he startles when she comes up behind him in the kitchen. He snaps at her, then apologizes, ashamed and confused by how on edge he feels.

Returning to work is worse than he expects. The hotel, once familiar, now feels full of blind corners and unsecured doors. He starts scanning the lobby, the elevators, the parking lot, the stairwells. He watches hands, waistbands, heavy coats, anyone lingering too long near the desk. Staff members notice that he has become more rigid about security procedures. He insists no one take trash out alone after dark. He changes closing routines, installs brighter lights, checks surveillance monitors himself. These changes are sensible on the surface, but he knows his vigilance has gone beyond caution. He no longer walks through the side lot where the robbery occurred. If he has to leave after sunset, he asks an employee to accompany him, pretending it is for their benefit.

He also begins avoiding parts of his old life that remind him of his vulnerability. He stops carrying cash. He refuses to stop for gas at night. He declines dinner invitations if driving home will be late. His wife wants to take a weekend trip, but he finds reasons to postpone it; unfamiliar parking garages and poorly lit sidewalks now feel intolerable. He used to enjoy chatting with guests and regular vendors. Now he keeps interactions brief, especially with men who resemble the robber in build or posture, though he knows this is irrational and dislikes what it brings out in him.

What troubles him most is how much he feels changed. He says he used to believe experience had made him harder to shake. Instead, he finds himself ambushed by fear in small moments: someone approaching too quickly in the lot, footsteps behind him, the beep of the office security panel, even the smell of damp concrete after rain. At home, he sits with his back to the wall in restaurants and scans entrances automatically. His wife says he is physically present but far away. He admits there are evenings when she is talking and he realizes he has not heard a word because he is back behind the hotel, pinned against the wall, waiting for the worst.

He tries to keep functioning by leaning harder into routine. He arrives early, checks everything twice, stays busy. From the outside he still looks like a competent manager nearing retirement, dependable as ever. But he describes living as if danger is always just outside the frame, ready to step forward again. Even in moments of calm, his body does not believe he is safe.
